verdict.why: Both halves of H1 are supplied for the stated object: $z(0) = -\partial_x \omega(0,0) = -\omega_0'(0)$ is exactly the definition evaluated at $t = 0$, with positivity named to hypothesis H2 of the citing node, and $C^1$ regularity of $t \mapsto -\partial_x \omega(t,0)$ is a genuine consequence of the local solution being classical (the equation gives $\partial_t \partial_x \omega$ continuously), not a placeholder. The only slack is the interval, $[0,T_{\max})$ supplied against $[0,T)$ needed, which is harmless provided the criterion is applied with $T \le T_{\max}$ as intended.

The source is hypothesis H2 of the citing node itself, which states $\omega_0$ is odd with $\omega_0'(0) < 0$ — exactly the needed hypothesis, and it is a condition on the initial datum $\omega_0$, so no transfer to a later time $t \in [0, T_{\max})$ is required. The extra regularity clause $\omega_0 \in H^s(\mathbb{S}^1)$, $s > 3/2$, is strictly more information than H2 asks for.

H2 is strictly stronger than H1 in the relevant respects and does contain "$\\omega_0 \\in H^s(\\mathbb{S}^1)$, $s > 3/2$" verbatim as a conjunct, so the needed regularity and range of $s$ are supplied for the same object $\\omega_0$; the extra conditions (odd, $\\omega_0'(0) < 0$) are harmless surplus. However, H2 is a hypothesis of `gclm.blowup` itself, which the citation resolves to only if the $s$ in H2 is the same $s$ the lemma is instantiated at, and that is not shown here.

H2 gives $\omega_0 \in H^s(\mathbb{S}^1)$ with $s > 3/2$, which is exactly H3 (H2 is strictly stronger, adding oddness and $\omega_0'(0) < 0$), but H3 is a hypothesis on the initial datum $\omega_0$ while the lemma is being applied to $\omega(t,\cdot)$ for $t \in [0, T_{\max})$; nothing in H2 supplies $\omega(t,\cdot) \in H^s$ at positive times, which needs a persistence-of-regularity statement (local well-posedness in $H^s$ on $[0,T_{\max})$).

The needed hypothesis $0 < a < 1/2$ is literally hypothesis H1 of the citing node's own statement, and it is a constraint on the fixed parameter $a$ rather than on the object $\omega(t,\cdot)$, so it holds uniformly for all $t \in [0, T_{\max})$ with no transfer required.
